prompt: A program logs through SLF4J and its classpath holds `slf4j-api` and nothing else to do with logging. What happens when it runs?
hint: The first run of Hello.java.

choices.text: Three warnings, then none of its lines
choices.why: Right. With no provider SLF4J falls back to a no-operation logger that discards everything, which is why those warnings are worth recognising.

choices.text: It throws an exception at the first call to getLogger
choices.why: SLF4J does not fail: a missing provider is a warning, and the program carries on.

choices.text: It writes every line to the console in a plain default format
choices.why: That is what Logback does with no configuration. With no backend at all there is nobody to write a line.

choices.text: It writes only the ERROR line, because errors are never discarded
choices.why: That was Log4j2 without a configuration file. The no-operation logger discards errors as well.

prompt: A program written against SLF4J writes its lines through Logback, and the team wants Log4j2 instead. What has to change?
hint: What differed between the runs of Hello.java?

choices.text: Replace every LoggerFactory call with the new library's own factory
choices.why: That is the work the facade exists to avoid. Code written against SLF4J never names the backend.

choices.text: Recompile against a different version of slf4j-api
choices.why: The API is the same whichever backend is used; the version of the facade does not choose the backend.

choices.text: Set a system property naming the backend when the JVM starts
choices.why: SLF4J finds its provider on the classpath. No property was set in any of the four runs of Hello.java.

choices.text: The dependencies: another provider on the classpath
choices.why: Right. Hello.java ran unchanged with Logback, Log4j2 and TinyLog; only the profile, and so the classpath, changed.

prompt: Match each jar in the bookshop's tree to what it does.
hint: One is the facade, one the backend, and two are bridges.

pairs.right: the interface the bookshop's code calls
formats each line and writes it
sends calls to the Log4j API to SLF4J

right_distractors: a second backend that writes beside Logback

prompt: Put the five levels in order, from the most talkative to the most serious.
hint: The root threshold in Boot sits in the middle.

prompt: The bookshop starts with `--logging.level.root=warn --logging.level.com.example.bookshop=info`. Which INFO lines does the start-up write?
hint: Look at the logger names in that run, not only at who wrote the code.

choices.text: Only the catalogue line, because CatalogueReport is the only class of the bookshop that logs at start-up
choices.why: The run showed four INFO lines. Three were written by Spring Boot under the application class's name.

choices.text: Every INFO line of the start-up, because a more specific setting replaces the root one for all loggers
choices.why: A setting for com.example.bookshop applies to the loggers under that name only; Hikari and Flyway stayed at WARN.

choices.text: The catalogue line and Boot's "Starting" and "Started" lines, which Boot logs under the name of BookshopApplication
choices.why: Right. A threshold filters by the logger's name, and the name is whatever the caller asked for, here the bookshop's own class.

choices.text: None, because the root threshold of WARN wins over any setting below it
choices.why: It is the other way round: the most specific name that has a setting decides.

prompt: Inside a loop with the threshold at INFO, what does `log.debug("Line " + line)` cost that `log.debug("Line {}", line)` does not?
hint: When is each string put together?

choices.text: The string is built even for a line thrown away
choices.why: Right. With placeholders the backend checks the threshold first and formats only the lines it keeps.

choices.text: The two print different text when the line is written
choices.why: They print the same line. The difference is in the work done when the line is not written.

choices.text: Concatenation cannot be used with SLF4J and does not compile
choices.why: It compiles: info takes a String, and a joined string is one.

choices.text: Placeholders skip evaluating the arguments when debug is off
choices.why: The arguments are evaluated either way; that is what the supplier form of the fluent API is for.

prompt: To log a caught exception with its stack trace, SLF4J expects it as the ___ argument, with no `{}` written for it.
A customer orders two copies of Frankenstein with one left, and gets a 409. If this were logged, which level fits?
hint: Who has to act on an ERROR?

choices.text: ERROR, because the order failed
choices.why: An ERROR asks somebody to act. A customer asking for more copies than exist is the application working, and the 409 already tells them.

choices.text: At most INFO, and OrderService does not log it at all
choices.why: Right. It is an ordinary business outcome; the response says it, and an ERROR here would wake whoever is on call.

choices.text: WARN, because it is unexpected and the application handled it
choices.why: It is not unexpected: refusing an order the stock cannot cover is one of the bookshop's rules.

choices.text: DEBUG, because only developers care about stock
choices.why: Stock running out matters to the business. The point is that it is not a failure of the application.

prompt: Why does RequestIdFilter call `MDC.remove("requestId")` in a `finally` block?
hint: Where does the thread go after the response?

choices.text: To free the memory the map uses
choices.why: The map is tiny. What matters is who uses the thread next.

choices.text: So that the header is removed from the response before it is sent
choices.why: The header was set on the response, not in the MDC; removing the MDC entry does not touch it.

choices.text: Because Logback refuses to write a line while an MDC key is set
choices.why: Logback writes lines with MDC keys set all the time; that is how the id reaches them.

choices.text: A pooled thread would carry this id into the next request
choices.why: Right. The MDC belongs to the thread, and a pooled thread outlives the request.

prompt: A client sends `X-Request-Id: two words`. What happens to that value?
hint: Read the pattern the filter matches against, and the curl run.

choices.text: It is too long, so the filter cuts it to eight characters
choices.why: Two words is short. The replacement is eight characters of a random UUID, not a cut of what was sent.

choices.text: It is kept, because the filter trusts whatever the caller sends
choices.why: The run showed `29aba6be` coming back, not `two words`.

choices.text: It is replaced, since the filter never accepts a space
choices.why: Right. Only letters, digits and hyphens are kept, so a value from outside cannot carry anything that would forge a line.

choices.text: The request is refused with a 400
choices.why: The request got a 200. The filter replaces a bad id; it does not reject the request.

prompt: When a request arrives with no usable id, how many characters long is the id RequestIdFilter makes up?
hint: `substring(0, 8)`.

prompt: What does `@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)` on RequestIdFilter change for a POST to /orders with no token?
hint: The last curl before the order.

choices.text: The 401 has no X-Request-Id, because Spring Security answers before any filter of the application runs
choices.why: The run showed `6bd16e4a` on the 401. The order of filters is exactly what @Order decides.

choices.text: The 401 still carries an id, since the filter runs first
choices.why: Right. HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE puts it ahead of the security filters, so even a refused request can be found in the log.

choices.text: The 401 carries the id, but only because Spring Security copies the header itself
choices.why: Spring Security knows nothing of this header; the bookshop's filter set it before the security chain ran.

choices.text: There is no response at all to a POST without a token
choices.why: There is: a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header, as lesson 15 showed.

prompt: OrderService starts sending a confirmation e-mail with `CompletableFuture.runAsync(...)`, and the e-mail code logs a line. What does that line show in the correlation slot?
hint: Whose map is the MDC?

choices.text: An empty `[]`, unless the code copied the MDC map to the other thread
choices.why: Right. The other thread starts with its own, empty MDC; getCopyOfContextMap and setContextMap carry it across.

choices.text: The request id, because the MDC is shared by every thread of the application
choices.why: The MDC is per thread. That is the property that keeps fifty concurrent requests apart.

choices.text: The id of whichever request that pool thread served last
choices.why: The filter removes the id in finally, and a pool thread that is not running a request has none.

choices.text: A new random id, made by RequestIdFilter for the other thread
choices.why: The filter runs once per HTTP request, on the request's thread. It never sees the other thread.

prompt: What does `logging.structured.format.console=ecs` change about the bookshop's log?
hint: Compare the order line before and after the json profile.

choices.text: The log is written to a file instead of the console
choices.why: It still goes to the console: the property ends in `.console`. What changes is the shape of each line.

choices.text: Only the bookshop's own lines become JSON; Spring's stay as text
choices.why: Every line became JSON, Spring's included; the 14 tagged COMMONS-LOGGING are Spring's.

choices.text: The lines are compressed before they are written
choices.why: Nothing is compressed; a JSON line is longer than the text one.

choices.text: Each event becomes one JSON object on a single line, MDC included
choices.why: Right. That is why `requestId` could be filtered on as a field rather than searched for as text.

prompt: The bookshop can write ECS, Logstash or GELF. What decides which one it should use?
hint: What changed between the ecs and the logstash run?

choices.text: ECS is for development and Logstash for production
choices.why: Neither is tied to an environment. Both are JSON for a collector, and the json profile is what keeps them out of development.

choices.text: Whatever collects the log, not the code that writes it
choices.why: Right. The logstash run changed one property; OrderService and the MDC did not change.

choices.text: Only ECS carries MDC entries such as requestId
choices.why: The Logstash line carried `requestId` too.

choices.text: Switching formats needs a change to the logging code in OrderService
choices.why: The switch was `--logging.structured.format.console=logstash` on the command line and nothing else.

prompt: Which of these should never be written to the bookshop's log? Choose all that apply.
hint: Credentials, and personal data the line does not need.

choices.text: The value of the Authorization header
choices.why: Right. Anybody who reads a token in a log can use it until it expires.

choices.text: The password typed in a failed login
choices.why: Right. A wrong password is often one character away from the right one.

choices.text: The id of the order that was placed
choices.why: An order id identifies a record, not a person or a secret; it is what makes the line useful.

choices.text: The customer's e-mail address, on every order line
choices.why: Right. Personal data the line does not need stays out; an opaque account id does the same job.

choices.text: The request id
choices.why: It was made to be logged: it carries no secret and no personal data.

prompt: In which jar did the Log4Shell vulnerability live?
hint: The backend, not an API.

choices.text: log4j-core, the Log4j2 backend that formats each message
choices.why: Right. Versions 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 of log4j-core expanded lookups found inside messages.

choices.text: slf4j-api, because every call passed through it
choices.why: The facade forwards the message untouched. The lookups happened in the code that formats it.

choices.text: log4j-api, the Log4j interface that the bookshop also carries
choices.why: The bookshop carries log4j-api and was not exposed: its calls go to Logback through log4j-to-slf4j.

choices.text: logback-classic, which the bridges sent every call to
choices.why: Logback has no message lookups; Boot applications on the default starter were not exposed.

prompt: In 2021, what did logging through SLF4J do for an application whose backend was Log4j2 2.14.1?
hint: Where were the lookups expanded?

choices.text: SLF4J filtered out messages containing `${`, so only Log4j2's own API was affected
choices.why: SLF4J does not inspect messages. It handed the attacker's string, unchanged, to whichever backend was behind it.

choices.text: They were safe, because a facade keeps the backend from seeing the original text
choices.why: The backend formats the original text; that is the only way it can write the line.

choices.text: Nothing: the facade passed the message to the same log4j-core
choices.why: Right. What the facade bought was the cure: moving to a fixed backend was a change of dependencies, with no class touched.

choices.text: They were safe as long as the code used `{}` placeholders instead of concatenation
choices.why: A placeholder's value is still part of the message log4j-core formatted, and the attacker's string usually arrived as that value.

prompt: Match each classpath to what `Hello.java` printed with it and no configuration file.
hint: Four runs of the same file.

pairs.right: three SLF4J warnings, and none of its lines
all four lines, one line each
only the ERROR, with the time in UTC
all four, each on two lines with the method name

prompt: A team moves the bookshop to TinyLog: they exclude the logging starter and add slf4j-tinylog. What does the bookshop lose?
hint: What did this lesson configure through Boot's properties?

choices.text: Nothing: Boot detects TinyLog and configures it like Logback
choices.why: Boot's logging support covers Logback, Log4j2 and java.util.logging, and nothing else.

choices.text: The level properties, the correlation pattern and the JSON formats
choices.why: Right. Those are Boot configuring its backend; with a backend Boot does not know, tinylog.properties does that job.

choices.text: The application stops compiling, because Spring's classes need Logback
choices.why: Spring's classes log through commons-logging and SLF4J; they compile and run with any provider.

choices.text: Only the ability to log exceptions with their stack traces
choices.why: TinyLog printed the stack trace in the Hello run.

prompt: Put in order what happens to OrderService's line, from the call to the text in app.log.
hint: The facade first, the threshold before the formatting.
items: OrderService calls log.info on its SLF4J Logger
SLF4J hands the call to its provider, Logback
Logback compares INFO with the threshold of the logger's name
Logback formats the message, filling each {} and reading requestId from the MDC
The line is written to standard output, which the shell sends to app.log
trap: Formatting before the threshold check would build every line, kept or not, which is the cost placeholders avoid.

prompt: A customer's checkout failed, and the support ticket quotes the `X-Request-Id` from the error response. What is the quickest way to everything the bookshop logged about it?
hint: The id was returned so that somebody could quote it.

choices.text: Search the log for the customer's name around the time of the call
choices.why: The order line holds an account name, not a name, and searching by time mixes in every other request of that minute.

choices.text: Search for the thread name from the error, then read every line of that thread
choices.why: A pool thread serves one request after another, so its lines belong to many customers.

choices.text: Turn logging up to DEBUG and ask the customer to try again
choices.why: That may help with the next attempt and tells nothing about the one that failed, which is already in the log.

choices.text: Search for that id, which every line of that request carries
choices.why: Right. That is the whole purpose of the filter and the correlation slot; in JSON it is even a field to filter on.

prompt: A new BookController method logs `log.info("Search for {}", q)` with the text a visitor typed. With the text format, what is the risk, and does the json profile change it?
hint: What did the filter refuse in X-Request-Id, and how does each format write a message that holds a newline?

choices.text: A line break in the text could add a fake line of its own; JSON escapes it, the text pattern does not
choices.why: Right. In the ECS output a newline inside a message is written as \n within one object, while the text pattern prints it as a real line break.

choices.text: Nothing, because a request id never goes in the log as it came
choices.why: That rule belongs to RequestIdFilter only. A search box value logged by another class goes through no filter.

choices.text: The search text could run as code inside Logback, as it did in Log4j2
choices.why: Logback has no message lookups. The risk with Logback is a forged line, not code being run.

choices.text: There is no risk, because `{}` placeholders escape whatever they are given
choices.why: Placeholders insert the value as it is; they escape nothing.

prompt: A library added to the bookshop logs an INFO line through the Log4j API, `LogManager.getLogger(...)`. Where does the line end up?
hint: Read the tree again: which Log4j jars are there, and which is absent?

choices.text: Nowhere, because log4j-core is not in the bookshop
choices.why: log4j-core would be a backend, and the bookshop does not need it: log4j-to-slf4j is the Log4j API's way out to SLF4J.

choices.text: Nowhere, because Log4j2 with no configuration keeps only ERROR
choices.why: That was Hello with log4j-core behind it. Here no Log4j2 backend runs at all, so its default never applies.

choices.text: In app.log, through log4j-to-slf4j, SLF4J and Logback
choices.why: Right. That bridge is why a library's choice of API does not decide where its lines go.

choices.text: In a separate file that the Log4j API creates beside app.log
choices.why: An API writes nothing; it hands each call to whatever is behind it.
